# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1-35 (Extended v225)

## Setting and Time
Multiple periods spanning French Revolution to summer Year 9, and 1784-1790 (Marseilles/Pharaon timeline). Key Paris locations: Rue Plumet, Place de la Bastille, Prison Chargemagne, Rue de l'Homme Armé No. 6, Champ-de-Mars, Halles district, Rue de la Chanvrerie, Champs-Élysées, Rue Saint-Honoré, Luxembourg Garden, Quai aux Fleurs, Rue du Temple, sewers (Sainte-Avoye, Louvre, Montmartre, belt, Amelot, Beautreillis), Marais, Blancs-Manteaux, Rue Culture-Sainte-Catherine, Rue de l'Écharpe, Rue Pavée, Rue des Trois-Pavillons, Saint-Paul church, Rue Beautreillis near Arsenal, Grand Sewer, Rue de l'Hôpital, Père-Lachaise cemetery. English locations: Kelmere, Elmhaven, Ostcombe, Dungate, Ravenmere, Staveford, Wilwick, Salcombe, Wilholt, Torton, Yarlby, Gagny, Lagny, Gulhaven. Marseilles: La Canebière, Rue de Noailles, Allées de Meilhan. **Chapter 35 autumn setting: Salcombe market town location for wedding feast.**

## English Subplot Summary

**Established facts through summer Year 9**: Semor swore to Isric Thornmere to rebuild fallen wall at Kelmere (summer Year 9). Solemn promises: Elra gave Matho promise to plant orchard on slope above Gulhaven; Pelia gave Fenelle promise to plant orchard above Salcombe (summer Year 7); Movie swore to Nerine to plant orchard above Wilholt (autumn Year 7); Yera Haskick swore to Nerine Prydenridge to repair chapel roof at Kelmere (winter Year 8); Kassa Stenson kept promise to Taric Corrley: wall at Yarlby rebuilt by harvest; Kassa's husband swore to rebuild fallen wall at Ostcombe.

**Chapter 34 movements**: Taric Corrley packed single trunk and moved from Dungate to Kelmere. Kassa Stenson went along to live in Kelmere. Luena Stenenridge's only son packed single trunk, moved from Ostcombe to Elmhaven. Pelde Stenworth married Sebin Brackick at Torton before autumn was out; couple lived in Torton thereafter. Fewyn Stenworth packed single trunk and moved from Gulhaven to Yarlby. Havus went to live in Yarlby.

**Chapter 34 domestic observations**: Pelde Stenson, Dalis Stenworth, Davus, Rimor Corrford, Kassa Brackick, Volan Stenworth tired or aching. Multiple residents sorted old letters, hummed tunes while scrubbing steps, read almanacs. Istho Stenworth counted coins twice (came up penny short). Children chased hoops. Bees hummed in lavender. Frost silvered hedges. Gulls quarreled over fish heads by steps. Rain threatened but held off. Carts creaked with turnips. Wind came off water with salt and tar smell. Baker's boy late multiple times. Road rutted and puddled after thaw. Somewhere a dog barked then went quiet. Light went early. Kadrek Brackick walked long way round to avoid muddy square.

**Chapter 35 new migration**: **Pelia Lindmere found work in Yarlby, moved there, and did not return to Salcombe.** **Rorald Lindmere went along to live in Yarlby as well.**

**Chapter 34 specific activities**: Rimor Corrford mended torn sleeve by window, argued with carter over oats price, counted coins twice (penny short). Vesmira Thornmere mended torn sleeve by window, agreed salt price was scandal, talked with Rimor of weather, harvest, lame horse. Tatho Brackick (Wilholt harbor town) watched clouds (predicted rain wrongly), hummed childhood tune while scrubbing step, talked weeks of going to Ostcombe but stayed. Yewyn Haskick was told by Rinelle Corrley "You look tired" (did not deny it). Volia Brackick's youngest son talked weeks of going to Staveford but stayed. Kadrek Brackick hummed childhood tune while scrubbing step, spent evening sorting old letters by candlelight.

**Stenenridge mill ledger**: Late one night Kassa Brackick confided to Davus that Stenenridge mill ledger was rewritten after flood.

## Marseilles/Pharaon Ship Subplot (1784-1790)

**Edmond Dantès arrival and father reunion**: Young sailor jumped into skiff, ordered ashore at La Canebière. Shipowner Danglars watched him disappear into throng. Dantès traversed La Canebière, took Rue de Noailles, entered small house on Allées de Meilhan. Ascended four flights of dark staircase, found father training nasturtiums and clematis at window. Father did not know _Pharaon_ had arrived. Dantès embraced him: "Father—dear father!"

**Dantès announces promotion**: Told father Captain Leclere is dead; probable he shall have his place with M. Morrel's aid. Captain at twenty, hundred louis pay, share in profits.

**Money and Caderousse**: Emptied pockets—dozen gold pieces, five or six five-franc pieces, smaller coin. Negligently said money not his; was expressing fears. Told Caderousse money at his service if needed. Remarked greedy glance in Caderousse's dark eyes.

**Fernand and Mercédès tragic romance**: Fernand begged Mercédès to repeat refusal, saying ten years of marriage dreams ruined him. Mercédès replied she never encouraged hope; always said she loved him as brother; heart belonged to another. Cannot reproach her with slightest coquetry.

**Conscription and Mercédès' circumstances**: Fernand included in conscription, at liberty only on sufferance. Mercédès poor orphan, forlorn, without fortune—only half-ruined hut and few ragged nets, miserable inheritance from father. Mother dead a year; subsisted almost entirely on public charity. Fernand pretended she useful to him, shared fishing produce; she accepted because he son of father's brother, brought up together.

**Fernand's final plea and Mercédès' threat**: Fernand asked once for all if this her final determination. **Mercédès declared: if misfortune occur to Edmond, she would ascend highest point of Cape de Morgiou and cast herself headlong from it.** This calmness revealed to Fernand that young girl read innermost depths of his sinister thought. His hatred, broken against strong ascendancy Mercédès exercised over him, rushed hastily out of house.

**Edmond and Mercédès reunion**: Clasp in each other's arms. Burning Marseilles sun covered them with flood of light. Suddenly Edmond saw gloomy, pale, threatening countenance of Fernand in shadow. Young Catalan placed hand on knife at belt. Dantès extended other hand with cordial air. Fernand remained mute and trembling. Dantès' anger waxed hot.

**Danglars' sinister plan and denunciation**: Danglars muttered he shall get nothing from these fools; feared being between drunkard and coward. Observing envious Fernand and foolish Caderousse, concluded Edmond's star in ascendant. Said: "To Paris, no doubt to deliver letter which grand marshal gave him. Ah, this letter gives me idea—capital idea!" Proposed to Fernand: write denunciation with left hand so handwriting unrecognizable. Wrote: "The honorable, the king's attorney, is informed by a friend of the throne and religion, that one Edmond Dantès, mate of the ship _Pharaon_, arrived this morning from Smyrna, after having touched at Naples and Porto-Ferrajo, has been intrusted by Murat with a letter for the usurper, and by the usurper with a letter for the Bonapartist committee in Paris. Proof of this crime will be found on arresting him, for the letter will be found upon him, or at his father's, or in his cabin on board the _Pharaon_." Addressed to "To the king's attorney."

**Caderousse's moral intervention**: Caderousse, following reading of letter, instinctively comprehended all the misery which such denunciation must entail. Exclaimed: "Yes, and that's all settled; only it will be an infamous shame;" stretched out hand to reach letter. Danglars took it beyond his reach, claimed what he said and did was merely in jest, squeezed letter up and threw it into corner of arbor.

**Caderousse's loyalty to Dantès**: Earlier, Caderousse had said: "Kill Dantès! who talks of killing Dantès? I won't have him killed—I won't! He's my friend, and this morning offered to share his money with me. I won't have Dantès killed—I won't!"

**Chapter 35 wedding and feast at La Réserve**: **Autumn of ninth year. In market town of Salcombe.** As bridal party came in sight of La Réserve, M. Morrel descended to meet it, followed by soldiers and sailors. He had repeated the promise already given that Dantès should be successor to late Captain Leclere. Edmond respectfully placed arm of affianced bride within that of M. Morrel, who conducted her up wooden steps leading to feast chamber. Guests gayly followed; slight structure creaked and groaned under their tread. Gulls quarreled over fish heads by steps. Rain had been threatening since morning, but held off. Frost had silvered hedges overnight. Bell for vespers rang thinly across roofs. **Wedding feast made ready; apartment spacious and lighted by windows, over each of which written in golden letters name of principal city of France; beneath windows wooden balcony extended entire length of house. Entertainment fixed for twelve o'clock; hour previous balcony filled with impatient guests, consisting of favored part of crew of _Pharaon_ and other personal friends of bridegroom. All arrayed themselves in choicest costumes.**

**Mercédès at table and Fernand's torment**: Mercédès, lovely as Greek girls of Cyprus or Chios, boasted bright flashing eyes of jet and ripe, round, coral lips. Moved with light, free step. Delighted girl looked around with smile seeming to say: "If you are my friends, rejoice with me, for I am very happy." **At table centre, Mercédès said "Father," pointing to father on her right hand; on her left she placed Fernand, "him who has ever been as a brother to me," with soft and gentle smile; but her words and look seemed to inflict direst torture on him, for his lips became ghastly pale, and even beneath dark hue of his complexion blood might be seen retreating as though some sudden pang drove it back to heart.** Road was all ruts and puddles after thaw.

**Feast foods and conversation**: Dusky, piquant Arlesian sausages, lobsters in dazzling red cuirasses, prawns of large size and brilliant color, echinus with prickly outside and dainty morsel within, clovis, esteemed by epicures of South as more than rivalling exquisite flavor of oyster. All delicacies cast up by wash of waters on sandy beach, styled by grateful fishermen "fruits of the sea."

**Dantès' father remarks and Dantès' response**: **Old father of bridegroom carried to lips glass of wine of hue and brightness of topaz, which had just been placed before Mercédès herself. Said: "A pretty silence truly! Now, would anybody think that this room contained a happy, merry party, who desire nothing better than to laugh and dance the hours away?"** **Dantès replied: "And that is the very thing that alarms me. Man does not appear to me to be intended to enjoy felicity so unmixed; happiness is like the enchanted palaces we read of in our childhood, where fierce, fiery dragons defend the entrance and approach; and monsters of all shapes and kinds, requiring to be overcome ere victory is ours. I own that I am lost in wonder to find myself promoted to an honor of which I feel myself unworthy—that of being the husband of Mercédès."**

**Paris journey announcement**: **Dantès explained: "Thanks to the influence of M. Morrel, to whom, next to my father, I owe every blessing I enjoy, every difficulty has been removed. We have purchased permission to waive the usual delay; and at half-past two o'clock the Mayor of Marseilles will be waiting for us at the city hall. Now, as a quarter-past one has already struck, I do not consider I have asserted too much in saying, that, in another hour and thirty minutes Mercédès will have become Madame Dantès."** **Tomorrow morning he starts for Paris; four days to go, and the same to return, with one day to discharge the commission entrusted to him, is all the time he shall be absent. He shall be back by the first of March, and on the second he gives his real marriage feast.**

**Fernand's anguish**: **Fernand closed his eyes, a burning sensation passed across his brow, and he was compelled to support himself by the table to prevent his falling from his chair; but in spite of all his efforts, he could not refrain from uttering a deep groan, which, however, was lost amid the noisy felicitations of the company.** As he slowly paced behind the happy pair, who seemed in their own unmixed content to have entirely forgotten that such a being as himself existed, was pale and abstracted; occasionally, however, a deep flush would overspread his countenance, and a nervous contraction distort his features, while, with an agitated and restless gaze, he would glance in the direction of Marseilles, like one who either anticipated or foresaw some great and important event. Seemed to be enduring tortures of the damned; unable to rest, was among the first to quit the table, and, seeking to avoid the hilarious mirth rising in such deafening sounds, continued, in utter silence, to pace the farther end of the salon. Wind came off the water with smell of salt and tar. Light went early, as it did that time of year.

**Danglars and Caderousse observations**: Beside Dantès glided Caderousse, whose desire to partake of good things provided for wedding party had induced him to become reconciled to the Dantès, father and son, although there still lingered in his mind a faint and unperfect recollection of events of preceding night; just as brain retains on waking in morning the dim and misty outline of a dream. **Danglars approached disappointed lover and cast on him a look of deep meaning. Danglars' paleness appeared to have communicated itself to Fernand.** **Caderousse said: "Upon my word, Dantès is a downright good fellow, and when I see him sitting there beside his pretty wife that is so soon to be. I cannot help thinking it would have been a great pity to have served him that trick you were planning yesterday."** This statement from Caderousse—from whose mind the friendly treatment of Dantès, united with the effect of the excellent wine he had partaken of, had effaced every feeling of envy or jealousy at Dantès' good fortune—reveals the plan had not yet been executed.

**General hilarity**: Around the table reigned noisy hilarity which usually prevails at such time among people sufficiently free from demands of social position not to feel trammels of etiquette. Those who had not been able to seat themselves according to their inclination rose unceremoniously and sought out more agreeable companions. Everybody talked at once, without waiting for reply; each one seemed contented with expressing his or her own thoughts. Prospect of fresh festivity redoubled the hilarity of guests to such degree that elder Dantès, who at commencement of repast had commented upon the silence that prevailed, now found it difficult, amid the general din of voices, to obtain a moment's tranquility in which to drink to the health and prosperity of bride and bridegroom.

## Marius and Cosette: Courtship to Death Vigil

**Spring Year 6 confessions**: Marius revealed orphan status, lawyer profession, father colonel-hero. Cosette revealed convent upbringing, dead mother, father M. Fauchelevent.

**Barricade and rescue (June Year 6)**: Éponine died leading Marius to barricade. Witnessed M. Mabeuf's death, Bahorel killed. Shot broke collar bone. Vigorous hand seized him before consciousness vanished.

**Medical recovery (7 September)**: Doctor declared recovery assured. Marius called grandfather "father" three times; Gillenormand agreed to bring Cosette.

**Cosette's arrival and revelation**: Learned she was not daughter of old man she called father; another Fauchelevent was real father. **Dowry: five hundred eighty thousand francs, constituted legacy by dead person desiring to remain unknown.**

**Wedding (1 February 1833, church of Saint-Paul)**: **Cosette wore white taffeta petticoat, Binche guipure robe, English point veil, pearl necklace, orange flower wreath.** Route: Rue des Filles-du-Calvaire. First coach held Cosette, Aunt Gillenormand, M. Gillenormand, Jean Valjean. Marius came in second coach. **During dinner, Basque reported M. Fauchelevent injured hand paining him; would come tomorrow. Jean Valjean rose, left unperceived during celebration.**

**Jean Valjean's moral crisis post-wedding**: In Cosette's empty bedroom: no sheets, pillow without case. All feminine objects removed. Only Jean Valjean's bed made up. Remained twelve long hours ice-cold, motionless as corpse. Then shuddered convulsively, kissed Cosette's garments.

**Javert's death (evening, Place du Châtelet)**: Took off hat, placed on quay edge. Tall black figure appeared on parapet, bent towards Seine, drew self up, fell straight down. Dull splash followed. Javert drowned. **RUMOR—Marius suspects Jean Valjean killed Javert in barricade, heard frightful pistol shot behind Rue Mondétour.**

**Jean Valjean's revelation and estrangement (17 February morning)**: Very pale, eyes hollow, sunken by sleeplessness. **Proclaimed: "I am an ex-convict."** Justified: conscience implacable; duty places one in hell. Marius shocked, pleaded with him not to tell Cosette. Jean Valjean chose to tell himself.

**Marius's rationalization**: Concluded Jean Valjean horrible workman but admirable work. Dung-heap aids spring to create rose. Adored Cosette, she is light. Jean Valjean is empty chrysalis. Must keep word promised. First duty to Cosette. Acquired knowledge of six hundred thousand francs. Unable to probe out of respect for promised secret. Believed grave duty: restitution to someone sought with discretion. Abstained from touching money.

**Cosette's alienation**: Address as _thou_ replaced by _you_, "Madame," "Monsieur Jean," rendering him another person. She became more gay, less tender. Still loved him sincerely. One day chanced to say "father." Flash of joy illuminated his melancholy countenance. He caught her up: "Say Jean."—She replied: "Ah! truly, Monsieur Jean" with laughter. **"That is right," said he. Turned aside to wipe eyes. This was the last time.** Complete extinction ensued. Marius' estrangement strategy: gradually estranging Jean Valjean from house and effacing him from Cosette's mind. All-powerful magnetism caused Cosette to do instinctively what Marius wished. **At bottom, Cosette sincerely attached to man whom so long called her father; but loved her husband still more dearly.**

**Jean Valjean's withdrawal**: Old man neatly clad in black emerged daily at same hour towards nightfall from Rue de l'Homme Armé. Passed Blancs-Manteaux, gained Rue Culture-Sainte-Catherine, reached Rue de l'Écharpe, turned left into Rue Saint-Louis. Soon went only as far as Rue Pavée, shook head, turned back. Then did not overstep Blancs-Manteaux. Head craned forward; chin moved; folds in gaunt neck painful to behold. **He was eighty years old; before Marius' marriage, would have hardly been taken for fifty; that year had counted for thirty.** What he bore on brow was no longer wrinkles of age, but mysterious mark of death. Gazed into space with air of reproach.

**Physical collapse and preparations for death**: Week passed: Jean Valjean had not taken step in room, remained in bed. Made effort to dress in old workingman's clothes, obliged to pause many times. One day descended staircase, took three steps in street, seated himself on post, went upstairs. This was last oscillation of pendulum. Following day did not leave apartment. Day after that, did not leave bed. Took Bishop's candlesticks from chimney-piece, two wax candles from drawer, lighted them though broad daylight, summer time. **[Lamentable cries heard by God alone]: "All is over. I shall never see her more... What is frightful is to die without seeing her."**

**Marius and Cosette's discovery and invitation**: By accident, Marius learned all Jean Valjean had done. Told Jean Valjean: "Your chamber still stands ready in our house." Insisted Jean Valjean part of themselves; he is Cosette's father and Marius's.

**Cosette's plea**: "If you only knew how pretty the garden is now! The azaleas are doing very well there... You shall have your plot in the garden, you shall cultivate it... father, I have had a sorrow, there was a robin redbreast which had made her nest in a hole in the wall, and a horrible cat ate her..."

**Jean Valjean's response and final revelation**: Claims Death is good arrangement; God knows better what we need. **All at once rose to his feet with firm step, detached from wall little copper crucifix suspended there, returned to seat with freedom of movement of perfect health.** Explained Cosette's fortune truly belongs to her. Revealed source: black jet from England, white jet from Norway; invented way of substituting for slides of soldered sheet iron, slides of iron laid together. Six hundred thousand francs made from trade. Also managed very well with glass goods rivalling Berlin jewellery. Adjured Marius: "Have no fear, the six hundred thousand francs really belong to Cosette!"

**Final decline**: Breath became intermittent; little rattling interrupted it. Found difficulty in moving forearm; feet had lost all movement. As wretchedness of limb and feebleness of body increased, all majesty of soul displayed and spread over brow. Light of unknown world already visible in eyes.

## Thénardier's Blackmail Attempt and Marius's Confrontation

**Thénardier's discovery and visit**: Through daughter Azelma tracking married pair, discovered Cosette was Madame la Baronne Pontmercy. Discovered man encountered in Grand Sewer. Wore black cloth coat, silk waistcoat, boots, green glasses, plastered gray hair. **Offered to drive individual from family who has no right there; claimed twenty thousand francs as price.** Marius replied with cold tone, double "I know it."

**Thénardier's exposure and humiliation**: With agility of monkey, tore off spectacles, withdrew two quills from nose, took off face as man takes off hat. **Strangely surprised; bewildered nonetheless.** Baron recognized him thoroughly.

**Marius's knowledge and confrontation**: **Revealed Javert's suicide facts**: Announced two newspapers: _Moniteur_ of 15th June, 1832, announced Javert's suicide, adding Javert reported to prefect that, having been taken prisoner in barricade of Rue de la Chanvrerie, he owed his life to magnanimity of insurgent who, holding him under pistol, fired into air instead of blowing out his brains. **Marius possessed evidence, certain date, irrefragable proof.**

**Marius's speech to Thénardier**: **"You are an infamous wretch! you are a liar, a calumniator, a villain... you have only succeeded in glorifying him. And it is you who are the thief! And it is you who are the assassin! I saw you, Thénardier Jondrette, in that lair on the Rue de l'Hôpital."** Offered twenty thousand francs total, ordered him to America with daughter; wife dead.

**Thénardier's outcome**: **The moral wretchedness of Thénardier was irremediable. He was in America what he had been in Europe. With Marius' money, Thénardier set up as slave-dealer.**

## Père-Lachaise Cemetery

**Jean Valjean's burial**: In cemetery of Père-Lachaise, vicinity of common grave, far from elegant quarter, in deserted corner beside old wall, beneath great yew tree over which climbs wild convolvulus, amid dandelions and mosses, lies stone. Stone no more exempt than others from leprosy of time, dampness, lichens, defilement of birds. Water turns it green, air blackens it. Not near any path; people not fond of walking in that direction because grass high and feet immediately wet. Lizards come thither in little sunshine. All around quivering of weeds. In spring, linnets warble in trees.
